section_summary: This section documents a wave of letters and petitions urging President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State Cordell Hull to halt American exports of arms, scrap iron, oil, gasoline, aircraft and other war-supporting materials to Japan during its invasion of China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could not be invoked without a presidential finding of a state of war, would restrict exports to both China and Japan, and did not authorize embargoes on most raw materials. The section also contains reports on German bombers shipped to Japan, the bombing of Canton, extensive petition signatures, and internal correspondence concerning a presidential reply to Yenching University president J. Leighton Stuart.

subfiles.title: Reply to the Reverend Jacob G. Brouwer on exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen states that a presidential proclamation recognizing a state of war would prohibit arms exports to both belligerents, but that no legal authority existed to stop exports to Japan alone. He says Roosevelt judged invocation contrary to American interests and supplies licensed-export totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding the Friends of China petition
subfiles.about: Forwards a petition signed at Silver Bay asking action against war-sustaining exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gillett sends the Friends of China petition from Silver Bay meetings, with 263 signatories, asking the President for consideration and action.

subfiles.title: Petition on the Japanese Invasion of China
subfiles.from: Friends of China at Silver Bay and petition signatories
subfiles.about: Requests measures to end American exports that supported Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The petition condemns Japan as the aggressor and argues that American scrap iron, oil, trucks, aircraft, bombs and shells were sustaining attacks on Chinese civilians. It asks Roosevelt to use every practicable direct and indirect means to stop the traffic, followed by numerous signatures and partial addresses.

subfiles.title: Reply to P. L. Gillett and the Friends of China
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Silver Bay petition concerning exports of war and other materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains the legal limits of the Neutrality Act and notes that it covered enumerated arms but not ordinary commodities. He gives export-license figures and recalls Hull's public condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Peabody's protest to Secretary Hull
subfiles.about: Protests the administration's failure to embargo scrap iron and oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Peabody argues Americans share guilt for Japanese bombing because supplies reach Japan, is disappointed in Hull and Roosevelt, and asks for decisive action.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Henry W. Peabody
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the administration's position on war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the Neutrality Act could bar arms only after a presidential proclamation and could not prohibit non-enumerated commodities. He emphasizes presidential discretion, provides export-license totals, and cites Hull's condemnation of bombing civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for enclosure 894.24/309
subfiles.about: Records the charging out of an enclosure from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: Charge slip for enclosure 894.24/309, charged to TS-Barlims on January 22, 1944.

subfiles.title: Wellesley professor's letter on American supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Challenges the discrepancy between Hull's peace program and continuing American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wellesley professor says the US furnished much of Japan's war matériel, quotes Madame Chiang on stopping scrap-iron exports, and warns of lasting hatred in China.

subfiles.title: The Bombing of Canton
subfiles.from: Canton Committee for Justice to China; prepared by the Reverend G. Baker
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese bombing of Canton and states the committee's five-point program.
subfiles.summary: Bulletin 'The Bombing of Canton' says attacks were indiscriminate against civilian targets and calls for Anglo-American action, boycott of Japan, aid to China and relief contributions.

subfiles.title: Reply to Professor Thompson
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers criticism of American exports sustaining Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Yost repeats that the President had declined to invoke the Neutrality Act after weighing American interests and that invocation would bar arms to both sides. He adds that cotton, scrap iron, oil and copper were outside the statutory arms list and could not legally be embargoed by executive action.

subfiles.title: Report of German bombers shipped to Japan
subfiles.from: Donald R. Heath, U.S. Embassy Berlin
subfiles.about: Reports an eyewitness account of Heinkel bombers leaving Hamburg aboard a Japanese steamer.
subfiles.summary: An American Army officer saw four Heinkel 111 bombers on a Japanese vessel leaving Hamburg August 6, the first authenticated eyewitness report of German aircraft shipped to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cynthia Pearl Maus's protest to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American sales of aircraft, gasoline and munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cynthia Pearl Maus condemns American participation in attacks on Chinese cities, invokes the Nine-Power Treaty, and asks Roosevelt to press for non-participation and mediate like Theodore Roosevelt.

subfiles.title: Reply to Cynthia Pearl Maus
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Maus's protest against material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains the proclamation requirement, the bilateral effect of an arms embargo and the statutory exclusion of ordinary commodities. He cites the President's judgment against invoking the act, gives export-license totals and repeats Hull's condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: S. M. D. Miller's protest against munitions exports
subfiles.about: Asks the Secretary of State to stop American munitions from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miller writes from Detroit that Japan uses American munitions against China, calling the trade un-Christian.

subfiles.title: Reply to S. M. D. Miller
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the United States had not prohibited munitions exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that no arms prohibition could operate without a presidential finding of war and that invocation would affect both China and Japan. He defends the President's discretion, gives export-license figures and recalls Hull's statements against the bombing of civilians.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum requesting a draft reply
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a reply for the President's signature.
subfiles.summary: White House memo refers J. Leighton Stuart's appeal on the Neutrality Act and China to State for a draft reply.

subfiles.title: J. Leighton Stuart's appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt to consider invoking the Neutrality Act to aid China against Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Stuart recalls Roosevelt's earlier sympathy for China and asks why the United States had not used the Neutrality Act despite Japan's undeclared war. He argues that Japanese conquest of North China threatened treaty obligations, Chinese independence and future peace throughout the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Submission of a draft presidential reply to Stuart
subfiles.about: Transmits a proposed reply to J. Leighton Stuart for presidential signature.
subfiles.summary: Hull sends a draft presidential answer to Stuart's July 15 letter and asks that the signed letter be returned for pouch to Peiping.

subfiles.title: Draft presidential letter to J. Leighton Stuart
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Stuart's appeal and encloses an explanation of the Neutrality Act policy.
subfiles.summary: Draft letter to Stuart affirms commitment to peace and treaties and encloses a statement on factors governing possible Neutrality Act application to the Far East.

subfiles.title: Statement on application of the Neutrality Act in the Far East
subfiles.about: Explains legal and policy considerations against applying the Neutrality Act to the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: The statement indicates that applying the act would prohibit arms to both China and Japan while leaving raw-material exports unaffected. It also cites the statute's peace-preserving purpose and Hull's public efforts to discourage civilian bombing and the sale of bombing aircraft.

subfiles.title: Instruction to deliver the President's letter to Stuart
subfiles.about: Directs confidential and secure delivery of Roosevelt's reply to J. Leighton Stuart.
subfiles.summary: Instruction transmits the President's response to Stuart for safe delivery, with copies for confidential information.

subfiles.title: Robert Stanley Ross's letter on American war supplies
subfiles.about: Asks whether American war supplies would continue to support Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: Robert Ross contrasts government responsibility with arms makers' interests and warns history might say China was murdered by Japan with American weapons.

subfiles.title: Reply to Robert Stanley Ross
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the administration's refusal to invoke the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential finding of war would impose an arms embargo on both China and Japan and that no legal authority otherwise existed to discriminate against Japan. He says the President judged invocation contrary to national interests and reports licensed-export values.

subfiles.title: First Christian Church appeal against supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges action to stop raw and finished products destined for Japanese military use.
subfiles.summary: First Christian Church's Cole says most Japanese war matériel came from the US and asks concrete restrictions rather than protests alone.

subfiles.title: Reply to Myron C. Cole
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers the church appeal concerning war and other materials shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost describes the Neutrality Act's proclamation mechanism and emphasizes that it did not authorize restrictions on commodities outside the official arms list. He defends Roosevelt's decision not to invoke the law and gives export-license figures for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Walter I. Fowle's appeal for an arms embargo
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo on arms and munitions exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Walter Fowle argues American supplies prolong Japan's war, dismisses the lack of a declaration as an excuse, and warns church people are losing confidence.

subfiles.title: Reply to Walter I. Fowle
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and policy position on exports of arms to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the Neutrality Act required a presidential proclamation and would prohibit arms exports to both combatants. He states that Roosevelt considered invocation contrary to national interests and supplies comparative licensed-export totals.

subfiles.title: Raphael Harwood Miller's inquiry to Hackworth
subfiles.about: Forwards a missionary's appeal and requests guidance on stopping supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miller describes Emma Lyon's educational service in China and asks what action is legally possible, recognizing the limits of an undeclared war.

subfiles.title: Copy of Miller's reply to Emma A. Lyon
subfiles.about: Explains Miller's understanding of the neutrality laws and voluntary boycott possibilities.
subfiles.summary: Miller tells Lyon undeclared wars leave American commerce free to aid the aggressor, suggests only a voluntary boycott could stop supplies, and promises to seek a State answer.

subfiles.title: Cover note supplying the omitted Lyon letter
subfiles.about: Sends a letter accidentally omitted from Miller's previous submission.
subfiles.summary: Carson apologizes that the Lyon letter should have accompanied Dr. Miller's communication the previous day.

subfiles.title: Hackworth's reply to Raphael Harwood Miller
subfiles.about: Explains that the State Department lacked authority to stop exports of gasoline, oil, scrap iron and cotton to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hackworth confirms Miller's conclusion that the Department could do nothing about the specified commodities. He explains the Neutrality Act's war-finding requirement and its limitation to arms, ammunition and implements of war, enclosing the statute, a pamphlet and Lyon's letter.

subfiles.title: White House return of signed Stuart letter
subfiles.about: Returns Roosevelt's signed letter to J. Leighton Stuart for diplomatic transmission.
subfiles.summary: McIntyre returns the President's signed draft sent with Hull's August 18 letter for transmission as proposed.

subfiles.title: Harry R. Sheppard's request for a policy statement
subfiles.about: Requests information for constituents protesting scrap-iron and other exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sheppard reports many constituent communications, especially from church people angry at shipments used against Chinese civilians, and asks for a policy statement.

subfiles.title: Hull's reply to Harry R. Sheppard
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed explanation of the Neutrality Act and scrap-iron exports for use with constituents.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that invoking the act would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan but that Roosevelt judged such action contrary to American interests. He stresses that scrap iron was outside the statutory arms list, notes the absence of embargo authority and repeats his condemnation of civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: Omer T. Fletcher's appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Urges the President to end American exports that helped Japan wage war against China.
subfiles.summary: Omer Fletcher lists steel, pig iron, copper, oil, automobiles and machinery supplied to Japan, and appeals for action while praising Roosevelt's peace efforts.

subfiles.title: Reply to Omer T. Fletcher
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal limits on restricting exports and acknowledges Fletcher's praise of Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the Neutrality Act depended on a presidential finding of war, applied to both belligerents and did not cover ordinary commodities. He gives licensed-export totals and conveys appreciation for Fletcher's remarks about Roosevelt's work for world peace.

subfiles.title: Representative Knute Hill's appeal to recognize existing wars
subfiles.about: Urges formal recognition of wars in Spain and the Far East so the Neutrality Act can be enforced.
subfiles.summary: Representative Knute Hill says states of war exist in China and Spain despite formalities and asks Hull to recognize them and halt raw materials and war supplies.

subfiles.title: Hull's reply to Representative Hill
subfiles.about: Contrasts the Neutrality Act's operation in Spain with the administration's policy in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Spain arms exports were already prohibited but the statute does not cover other materials; Roosevelt declined to invoke the act in East Asia; no authority over raw materials generally.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Belcher's appeal to invoke the Neutrality Act
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt to end war-sustaining trade with Japan by invoking the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Belcher argues continuing commerce makes the US a partner in Japan's destruction, and sees invoking the Neutrality Act as the means to end it.

subfiles.title: Reply to Harry B. Belcher
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Belcher's request that Roosevelt invoke the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential finding would prohibit arms to China as well as Japan and that no legal authority otherwise permitted a unilateral embargo. He defends Roosevelt's exercise of discretion and gives export-license totals for both countries.

subfiles.title: J. Fullerton Gressitt's letter from Japan
subfiles.about: Argues from personal observation in Japan that the Neutrality Act or an oil embargo should be used to stop the invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Gressitt describes Japanese mobilization, propaganda concerning Chiang Kai-shek and suppression of information about atrocities at Nanking and other captured cities. He contends that the invasion was effectively a declared war and urges an immediate embargo on oil and gasoline, which he believes would halt Japanese operations.

subfiles.title: Instruction concerning a reply to J. Fullerton Gressitt
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Asks the Tokyo consular officer to provide Gressitt with the standard explanation of American neutrality policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department encloses Gressitt's letter, the Joint Resolution and a pamphlet, suggesting language explaining why the act had not been invoked. The proposed reply stresses that oil and gasoline were not statutory arms and that no existing law authorized their prohibition.

subfiles.title: American Committee letter to Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Announces separate delivery of the booklet America's Share in Japan's War Guilt.
subfiles.summary: Price asks Hamilton to give careful, responsible consideration to the complimentary copy of the committee booklet.

subfiles.title: American Committee letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Sends Hull a complimentary copy of America's Share in Japan's War Guilt under separate cover.
subfiles.summary: Price calls the booklet a treatment of one of the most important foreign-policy issues and asks Hull's careful attention.
